sources.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume)
sources.locator: Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Eqs. (5.1)-(5.30), printed pages 1-7 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 87-93): harmonic oscillator, linear drag, damping coefficient, characteristic equation, free and forced solutions, response function, Green's function; Chapter 5 Section 5.3, Eqs. (5.52)-(5.57), printed pages 12-14 (PDF pages 99-101): harmonic balance and the reduced (averaged) equations; Chapter 10 Sections 10.2-10.3, Eqs. (10.28)-(10.42), printed pages 5-8 of Chapter 10 (PDF pages 241-244): action variable and adiabatic invariance. Read at these sections from the local copy retained with the run.

contents.name: Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Eqs. (5.1)-(5.4): harmonic oscillator equation and its general amplitude-phase solution
contents.support: The model m q''+eta q'+kappa q=F(t) and its solution families are the definitions and classification of the cited items, made explicit with all domains and regularity.

contents.name: Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Eqs. (5.5)-(5.9): linear drag, damping coefficient delta, characteristic equation lambda^2+2 delta lambda+omega_0^2=0 and the three solution cases
contents.support: The discriminant classification and the damped oscillatory family e^{-delta t}(u cos omega' t+v sin omega' t) are exactly clauses 1-3 for k>0; the source's delta, omega_0 are gamma, omega_0 here.

contents.name: Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Eqs. (5.10)-(5.12): exponential decay of free oscillations with time constant tau=1/delta and the quality factor
contents.support: The exponential-decay conclusion for c>0, k>0 is the corollary, with explicit per-case bounds; the Q-factor discussion itself is not a promised claim of this page.

contents.name: Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Eqs. (5.13)-(5.18): the forced equation, response function chi(omega) and forced amplitude (5.18)
contents.support: The steady response Re(f0 e^{i Omega t}/D) and its modulus reproduce (5.16)-(5.18) with D=k-m Omega^2+i c Omega; the source uses the engineering sign convention, noted in the item.

contents.name: Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Eqs. (5.19)-(5.22): resonance value at omega=omega_0, Q-factor ratio and FWHM
contents.support: The resonance peak and its location are absorbed into the amplitude-maximum proposition; the FWHM formula is not a promised claim of the design and is not built.

contents.name: Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Eqs. (5.23)-(5.30): temporal Green's function, response to a unit pulse and the convolution representation
contents.support: The convolution formula (5.27) and the pulse response (5.30) are the mathematical content of the variation-of-constants theorem, with the kernel identified as the homogeneous solution g(0)=0, g'(0)=1/m.

contents.name: Chapter 5 Section 5.3, Eqs. (5.52)-(5.57): harmonic balance and reduced equations obtained by averaging over one period
contents.support: The source's first-order averaged (RWA) equations are the motivation for the averaging datum; the theorem replaces the first-order truncation by the exact conjugation identity and a quantified order-epsilon bound.

contents.name: Chapter 10 Sections 10.2-10.3, Eqs. (10.28)-(10.42): slow parameter variation, averaged energy-change identity and adiabatic invariance of the action
contents.support: The action variable (10.39) and the averaged conclusion (10.42) are the model context of the adiabatic branch datum; the local theorem replaces the averaging step by the exact identity (I+epsilon g)'=epsilon^2(...) and gives a uniform finite-horizon bound.

sources.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, January 2015 version)
sources.locator: Section 4.5.1, printed pages 105-108: the simple harmonic oscillator in action-angle variables; Section 4.6, Eqs. (4.148)-(4.158), printed pages 113-115: adiabatic invariants with the author's explicit remark that stricter proofs are deferred to the literature; Section 2.6, printed pages 37-45: linearization around equilibria and normal modes. Read at these sections from the local copy retained with the run.

contents.name: Section 4.5.1, printed pages 105-108: action I=E/omega of the simple harmonic oscillator
contents.support: The harmonic-oscillator action computation is the concrete model behind the branch datum; no separate action-angle construction item is promised on this page.

contents.name: Section 4.6, Eqs. (4.148)-(4.158): energy change E-dot=(partial H/partial lambda) lambda-dot, the action I=(1/2 pi) closed integral p dq, and the averaged statement <I-dot>=0
contents.support: The source's honest averaged argument is the second independent treatment of adiabatic invariance; the theorem's remark records that the uniform bound here replaces the averaging with an exact identity.

contents.name: Section 2.6, printed pages 37-45: linearization about an equilibrium and the small-oscillation equations
contents.support: The source's linearization setup (equilibrium, linearized equations, quadratic corrections) is the model context; the theorem supplies the explicit finite-time remainder bound the source does not state.

sources.title: I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09 Fall 2014, complete course text)
sources.locator: Chapter 5 Sections 5.1-5.3, Eqs. (5.19)-(5.28), printed pages 93-98: first-order perturbation theory, average over one period and secular changes; Chapter 7 Section 7.1.3, Eqs. (7.15)-(7.16), printed pages 147-148: the linearised forced damped oscillator, underdamped/critically damped/overdamped cases and the resonance of the steady state. Read at these sections from the local copy retained with the run.

contents.name: Chapter 5 Sections 5.2-5.3, Eqs. (5.22)-(5.28): splitting a perturbation into periodic and secular parts and averaging over one period
contents.support: The secular/periodic decomposition after one-period averaging is the third independent treatment of the averaging idea; the theorem's conjugation and Gronwall argument makes the comparison uniform and explicit.

contents.name: Chapter 7 Section 7.1.3, Eq. (7.16): underdamped, critically damped and overdamped linearised oscillator solutions and the transient plus steady forced motion
contents.support: The three solution cases match the discriminant classification for k>0, and the transient-plus-steady structure is the content of the sinusoidal-response theorem's clause 3.

contents.name: Chapter 7 Section 7.1.3, printed page 148: resonant behaviour of the steady state amplitude at Omega=omega_0
contents.support: The resonant behaviour is captured exactly by the resonant clause (c=0, Omega=omega_0) and quantitatively by the amplitude-maximum proposition for c>0.

sources.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition)
sources.locator: Chapter 2 Section 2.4, Theorem 2.10 and estimate (2.43), printed pages 45-48: smooth dependence and the variational equation; Chapter 3 Sections 3.1-3.2, printed pages 57-66: the matrix exponential, linear systems, the inhomogeneous equation (3.47) with Duhamel's formula (3.48) and Problem 3.7 (t^m e^{alpha t}->0); Chapter 8 Section 8.6, formulas (8.76)-(8.81), printed pages 224-230: decoupled harmonic modes. Read at these sections from the local copy fetched by source-fetch-check.

contents.name: Chapter 3 Section 3.1, matrix exponential and its properties; Section 3.2, inhomogeneous linear system (3.47) and Duhamel's formula (3.48)
contents.support: The corollary proves the variation-of-constants formula with the operator lemma and the convolution differentiation lemma; formula (3.48) is the source's statement of the same identity.

contents.name: Chapter 3 Section 3.2, Problem 3.7: lim t^m e^{alpha t}=0 for Re alpha<0
contents.support: The source's limit identity is the classical statement behind the double-root decay case; the corollary proves the real case directly from the exponential-series lower bound, so the problem is context rather than a premise.

contents.name: Chapter 2 Section 2.4, Theorem 2.10 with estimate (2.43): C^k dependence on the initial condition and the first variational equation
contents.support: The source's smooth-dependence theorem is the qualitative background of the linearization layer (already realised on the cm-math-dynamics page); the finite-time quadratic-remainder bound here is stronger and quantitative.

contents.name: Chapter 8 Section 8.6, formulas (8.76)-(8.81): decoupling M q''+W q=0 into harmonic modes
contents.support: The decoupled modal system is the supplier theorem of cm-math-dynamics; the corollary adds continuous forcing and the convolution solution mode by mode.
